nature-found-015.title: The ecosystem, from a rock's surface to the whole planet
nature-found-015.text: An ecosystem can be as small as the surface of a single rock or as large as the surface of the planet. That is a span of ten orders of magnitude, and one idea covers all of it. An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with their non-living surroundings, linked by flows of energy and nutrients. Plants are living, or biotic, parts; soil is a non-living, or abiotic, part. Energy enters when plants capture sunlight, a process traced in {{ref:nature-eco-190}}. Animals carry matter and energy onward by eating plants and one another. Other organisms break down dead matter and return its nutrients to the system. Some forces act from outside: climate shapes an ecosystem without being changed by it. Others act from within, such as the breakdown of dead matter and the mix of species present, which both shape the system and respond to it. No ecosystem stands still. Each is always recovering from past upsets, and its ability to absorb a shock and keep working is the subject of {{ref:nature-eco-603}}. The word itself is young. British ecologist Arthur Tansley first used it in 1935; Arthur Roy Clapham coined it at his request. Ecosystems matter to the economy because they supply goods, such as water, food, fuel and medicinal plants. They also supply services, such as clean air and water, oxygen and crop pollination. Many are now degraded by soil loss, pollution, invading species and habitats broken into fragments. One that has lost its defining features is called collapsed.

nature-found-001.title: Biodiversity: the variety of life, and where it crowds
nature-found-001.text: Tropical forests cover less than one-fifth of Earth's land, yet they hold about 50% of the world's species. Life, in other words, is not spread evenly. Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth. Biologists most often describe it as the totality of genes, species and ecosystems of a region, and it can be measured at each of those levels. The tropics are richest, helped by the warm climate and high plant growth near the equator. How much life is there? Estimates by Mora and colleagues in 2011 put the count at about 8.7 million species on land and 2.2 million in the ocean. That variety does useful work. Many studies link more plant species to higher fodder and crop yields. It is also shrinking. Human activities are causing ongoing biodiversity loss, often called the Holocene or sixth mass extinction, and clearing habitat for farming is a key cause. In 2019 a global assessment by an intergovernmental science panel, described in {{ref:nature-gov-020}}, stated that the state of nature had deteriorated at an unprecedented and accelerating rate.

nature-found-004.title: Ecosystem services: the work nature does for people
nature-found-004.text: New York City had two ways to keep its water clean. It could build a filtration plant, estimated at $6–8 billion plus $300 million a year to run. Or it could restore its Catskill watershed, the land whose streams feed the city's supply, for an estimated $1–1.5 billion. The city chose the land, and the land did the plant's job for a fraction of the cost. That job is an ecosystem service: one of the many benefits people get from ecosystems. Others include pollination of crops, clean air, the breakdown of wastes and flood control. These services are vital for human well-being, giving direct and indirect benefits such as clean water, food and a steady climate. The term "environmental services" appeared in a 1970 report, and "ecosystem services" later became the standard term in science. In the early 2000s a United Nations initiative, covered in {{ref:nature-es-001}}, popularised sorting them into four groups: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural. Economists value these services in money using methods such as avoided cost, the cost of replacing a service, travel cost and surveys of what people would pay. A 1997 study put the value of the world's ecosystem services and the natural stocks behind them at US$16–54 trillion per year, averaging US$33 trillion. Some schemes now reward farmers or landowners for managing their land so that it keeps providing a service, an approach explored in {{ref:nature-mkt-136}}.

nature-found-010.title: Natural capital: nature as the stock behind the economy
nature-found-010.text: A well-kept forest or river can supply new trees or fish indefinitely. Overuse can shrink the timber or fish on offer for good. That difference sits at the heart of natural capital: the world's stock of natural resources, including rocks, soils, air, water and all living things. The term stretches an economic idea. Capital means resources that let you produce more resources, and natural capital applies that idea to the goods and services nature provides. Some of these assets give people goods and services at no charge, the ecosystem services that underpin the economy and society. Older economic thinking filed nature under "land", a factor with a fixed supply. Natural capital is different, because people can improve it or degrade it over time. E. F. Schumacher first used the term in 1973, in his book Small Is Beautiful. Herman Daly, Robert Costanza and other founders of a newer school, one that treats the economy as part of the ecosystem, developed it further. The OECD sees three main categories: natural resource stocks, land and ecosystems. Here is the catch. Natural capital's values are not counted in national income accounts or in GDP, the standard measure of a country's output. They have no prices, because they lie mostly outside markets. When businesses or people damage nature without being held to account, the harmed nature is called unpriced natural capital.

nature-eecon-208.title: Sustainability and the hard question of what to keep
nature-eecon-208.text: The word comes from the Latin sustinere, and "to sustain" can mean to maintain, support, uphold or endure. In its plainest sense, sustainability is the ability to keep going over a long time. Today it usually means a state in which environment, economy and society all continue to exist long into the future. Scholars usually split it along those lines into three dimensions: environmental, social and economic. Many definitions stress the environmental side, including tackling climate change and biodiversity loss. The economic side is controversial, and scholars debate it as a contest between weak and strong versions, explored in {{ref:nature-eecon-216}}. Sustainability is also a normative concept: it rests on what people value and want for the future. That makes it hard to measure. It is complex, it depends on context and it changes over time, and no fixed set of indicators exists. Critics call the idea vague, a mere buzzword, or an impossible goal, too loose to guide action. That charge has not been settled. UNESCO draws a useful line: sustainability is the long-term goal, and the pathways that reach it are a separate idea, covered in {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}.

nature-found-023.title: Environmental degradation: 70% of the land, already altered
nature-found-023.text: Since farming began over 11,000 years ago, people have altered about 70% of Earth's land surface. Along the way they have halved the global mass of vegetation. A 2021 study found that just 3% of Earth's land is still ecologically and faunally intact, with its ecosystems and animal life whole. This is environmental degradation: the worsening of the environment through lost resources such as clean air, water and soil, destroyed ecosystems and habitats, extinct wildlife, and pollution. A UN disaster-reduction body puts it more briefly, as a cut in the environment's capacity to meet social and ecological needs. Degradation runs down the natural capital that ecosystems hold. Some of it is plain to see, like deforestation. Some builds slowly, like plastic pollution, or heat-trapping gases pushing the climate toward tipping points. Its scale depends on more than the number of people. Consumption patterns matter, and so does how efficiently resources are used. Industrialised nations, consuming more per person, often leave a disproportionately large environmental footprint. The harm is not shared evenly either. Women's livelihoods, health, access to food, and access to water and energy are disproportionately hurt.

nature-found-022.title: The biosphere, from 19 km underground to 64 km up
nature-found-022.text: Life turns up at least 19 km underground and at least 64 km up in the atmosphere. It spreads from the polar ice caps to the equator. All of it together makes the biosphere: the sum of all the world's ecosystems, the zone of life on Earth. The biosphere joins every living thing with the rock, ice, water and air around it. For matter, it is almost a closed system, with little arriving or leaving. For energy, it is open. Living things that capture sunlight take in energy at around 100 terawatts. Geologist Eduard Suess coined the term in 1875, and Vladimir Vernadsky gave it its ecological meaning in the 1920s. Earth's biosphere is divided into large regions of similar life, and most of the richest lie near the equator.

nature-found-017.title: The Anthropocene: naming the human age
nature-found-017.text: The name joins Greek words meaning "human" and "new". The Anthropocene is a name for the period in which humanity has become a force that changes the whole planet. Eugene F. Stoermer first used the term informally in the 1980s, and Paul J. Crutzen popularised it. The signs are real. Rising carbon dioxide in the air, mostly from burning coal, oil and gas, is one geological mark of human activity. Human effects on biodiversity are another: extinction rates may run 100 to 1000 times the normal background rate, though the exact rate is disputed. Yet in 2024 the ICS and IUGS, the bodies that rule on geological time, rejected it as a formal new epoch after the Holocene. The vote did not dismiss human impact. It found that the epoch could not be pinned down geologically, and that the 1950 start date was prone to recency bias. Whether it is a valid formal unit remains disputed.

nature-found-005.title: Four kinds of help: sorting ecosystem services
nature-found-005.text: Not every benefit from nature works the same way. Some touch nearby people directly, like fresh water or food. Others act through general conditions, like a steady climate or soil held in place against erosion. To keep track, scientists sort ecosystem services into groups. The best-known scheme, from a United Nations assessment, uses four: regulating, provisioning, cultural and supporting. The provisioning group holds the products obtained from ecosystems, such as food, fresh water, wood, fibre and fuel. The regulating group comes from nature keeping its processes in check, through climate control, carbon storage, flood control and disease regulation. The supporting group, such as nutrient cycling and the making of soil, allows the other three to exist; it is the base on which the rest stand. Each group gets its own entry, beginning with {{ref:nature-found-009}}. An ecosystem need not offer all four kinds at once, but people usually benefit from a mix of them. Other schemes redraw the lines. To avoid counting the same benefit twice, a later study, covered in {{ref:nature-hist-001}}, replaced the base layer with habitat services. The Common International Classification for Ecosystem Services keeps the cultural and provisioning groups. It merges regulating and habitat services into one group, regulation and maintenance services.

nature-found-003.title: When more kinds of life mean more benefits
nature-found-003.text: Does a richer mix of life give people more? Many claims say so; some have been validated, some are wrong and some lack enough evidence. The firmest link runs through the services that keep nature's processes in check. Biodiversity supports those services, making ecosystems more stable, functional and adaptable. Different plants living together can play complementary roles, such as cycling nutrients and regulating water. This sharing of work, called niche complementarity, steadies ecosystems under climate stress.

nature-found-002.title: Why life crowds toward the equator
nature-found-002.text: Travel from the poles toward the tropics, and the number of species rises. This pattern is the latitudinal diversity gradient. Places at lower latitudes, nearer the equator, generally hold more species than places at higher latitudes. Several factors may contribute. Behind many of them lies one underlying cause: the higher average temperature at the equator. The rule has exceptions. Parasites do not seem to follow it, and soil bacteria are most diverse in temperate zones.

nature-found-009.title: Cultural services: beauty, belief and a day outdoors
nature-found-009.text: Some of nature's gifts cannot be eaten or burned. Cultural services are the non-material benefits of nature, such as recreation, beauty, learning and spiritual meaning. They include nature-based tourism and outdoor sports, nature's place in art and national symbols, and its religious or heritage value. They are hard to put in money terms. Critics go further, arguing that cultural values attach to unique landscapes and ways of seeing, not to measurable properties of ecosystems. Scholars still disagree over whether such values fit the ecosystem services approach at all.

nature-found-006.title: Provisioning services: food, timber and fuel from the wild
nature-found-006.text: In 2018, global production and trade of all major wood-based products reached their highest recorded values. Wood is one of many provisioning services: the products people obtain from ecosystems. They include food such as crops, seafood, game and spices. They also include raw materials such as lumber, skins, fuelwood, fodder for animals and fertilizer.

nature-found-016.title: Ecosystem goods: the material harvest of nature
nature-found-016.text: Water, food, fuel, building material and medicinal plants are all ecosystem goods: the tangible, material products of ecosystems. The category stretches further than it first seems. It also takes in less tangible items like tourism and recreation. It even includes wild genes used to improve domesticated plants and animals. Ecosystem goods overlap with provisioning services, but they are set apart from ecosystem services. In this view, services are improvements in the condition or location of things of value.

nature-found-007.title: Regulating services: bees, wetlands and coastal forests at work
nature-found-007.text: Bee pollination is needed for 15–30% of U.S. food production. That is a regulating service: a benefit people get from nature keeping ecosystem processes in check, such as climate, water and pests. Wetlands hold large amounts of water and release it slowly, making floods less likely. Coastal mangrove forests protect shorelines from erosion. Other examples are locking carbon away from the air, breaking down and detoxifying wastes and controlling pests and diseases.

nature-found-008.title: Supporting services: the slow work beneath everything else
nature-found-008.text: Every meal and every breath of oxygen traces back to processes few people notice. Supporting services are the background services, such as nutrient cycling and the slow making of soil, that make all other ecosystem services possible. They also include providing habitat, and the growth of new organic matter that forms the base of every chain of who eats whom. That growth, traced in {{ref:nature-eco-302}}, releases oxygen too. The effects of supporting services on people are indirect and play out over long periods.

nature-found-024.title: Freshwater depletion: a sliver of Earth's water, running short
nature-found-024.text: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh. Of that, 69% is frozen in ice caps, and only 30% is available for use. Freshwater depletion is the using up and spoiling of this limited supply, a major part of environmental degradation. About 85% of freshwater consumption goes to irrigation of farmland, golf courses and parks. An estimated one in three people worldwide already struggle with too little water.

nature-found-012.title: The Natural Capital Protocol: a common rulebook for business
nature-found-012.text: How should a company count its reliance on nature? The Natural Capital Protocol offers a standard answer. Released in July 2016 by the Natural Capital Coalition, now the Capitals Coalition, it helps organisations identify, measure and value their impacts and dependencies on natural capital. It brings existing tools together so that nature can enter strategic and operational decisions. It was developed by 38 organisations and is free to use under a Creative Commons licence.

nature-found-011.title: Finance chiefs pledge to count nature at Rio+20
nature-found-011.text: In June 2012, at the Rio+20 summit in Brazil, 40 chief executives from the finance sector signed the Natural Capital Declaration. They pledged to build natural capital into their products: loans, equity and fixed-income investments, and insurance. They also promised to bring it into accounting and reporting. One aim was to deepen understanding of how businesses depend on natural capital assets.

nature-found-014.title: Should nature carry a price tag
nature-found-014.text: Measuring the parts of natural capital is fairly straightforward. Putting a money value on them is not, and the argument over doing so is still open. Columnist George Monbiot derided valuation as comparing things that cannot be compared, and called the resulting figures "marmalade". Critics add that cultural values cannot carry a dollar amount, so valuation leaves parts of nature out. Defenders reply that valuation puts the environment on a fairer footing against commercial pressures. Valuing nature, they say, is not the same as turning it into money.

nature-found-013.title: SEEA: keeping national books on nature
nature-found-013.text: Can a country keep books on its environment as it does on its economy? The System of Environmental-Economic Accounting, or SEEA, is the international statistical standard for doing so. It tracks both the economy's impacts on the environment and the environment's contribution to the economy. The SEEA Central Framework reached its final form in February 2014. In March 2021 the UN Statistical Commission adopted a standard for ecosystem accounting, covering the extent, condition and services of ecosystems in physical and money terms. SEEA is a satellite of the UN's main system for measuring economies, described in {{ref:nature-econ-596}}, and shares its definitions, rules and boundaries.

nature-found-027.title: Eco-capitalism: putting markets to work for nature
nature-found-027.text: Eco-capitalism, or green capitalism, starts from a claim: nature is a form of capital on which all wealth depends. If that is true, markets should be used to solve environmental problems. Its supporters want governments to use market-based tools, such as a tax on carbon. A central aim is to correct a basic flaw in markets, in which polluters do not pay for the pollution they cause. Critics, including eco-socialists, doubt the approach. They argue that growth, and turning nature into a commodity, cannot easily be reconciled with sustainability.

nature-found-018.title: When did the human age begin
nature-found-018.text: Researchers cannot agree on when the human-shaped era of Earth's history began, and the candidates span thousands of years. William Ruddiman argued it began about 8,000 years ago, with farming and settled cultures. Others place it near the start of the Holocene, the present geological epoch, as early peoples cleared forests, hunted giant animals to extinction and spread invading species. Crutzen proposed the Industrial Revolution, and Lovelock proposed the first Newcomen steam engine, in 1712. In 2019 the Anthropocene Working Group proposed the mid-20th century. Then population, industry and farm chemicals surged, and atomic tests left radioactive debris in sediments.

nature-found-019.title: The Homogenocene: a world growing more alike
nature-found-019.text: Ecosystems around the world are growing more alike, mainly because people move species across the globe. Some species travel on purpose, as crops and livestock. Others travel by accident. Michael Samways first used a name for this age in 1999: the Homogenocene. It describes one face of the Anthropocene, the sameness that spreads when living things ride along with people.

nature-found-020.title: Assimilative capacity: how much waste nature can absorb
nature-found-020.text: A big, fast river can absorb more waste than a slow stream, because water lowers contaminant levels mainly by diluting them. That limit has a name. Assimilative capacity is how much pollution an environment can absorb without harm to it or to the people who use it. Nature absorbs pollutants by diluting and dispersing them, and by removing them through chemical or biological processes. A pollutant actually causes pollution only once that capacity is exceeded. Take salt. If an irrigation standard for salt is 450 mg/L, a water body's assimilative capacity is the salt that can be added before that level is passed. Governments use the idea to guide the sustainable growth of city regions and to judge how much pressure a region is under. Critics call its definition vague. They also say it wrongly implies that small amounts of pollution do no harm.

nature-found-026.title: Short-termism: the pull of the quick payoff
nature-found-026.text: Some actions take longer than one government's term to show results, and short-termism can undermine them. Short-termism is favouring quick profits and short-term results over long-term results and far-sighted action. It is linked to a thinking habit that prefers short-term payoffs to long-term rewards, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-065}}. Short-termism and consumerism are named among the barriers to sustainability.

nature-found-025.title: The triple planetary crisis: pollution, climate and vanishing species
nature-found-025.text: Over half of the world's economic output, measured as GDP, depends on nature, and over 1 billion people's livelihoods are tied to forests. That is why the UN warns of a triple planetary crisis: three linked global crises of pollution, climate change and biodiversity loss. Each is severe on its own. Pollution is the leading environmental cause of disease and death, linked to an estimated 9 million premature deaths in 2015. The climate crisis comes from too much heat-trapping gas in the atmosphere, bringing rising temperatures, sea-level rise and extreme weather. Up to one million plant and animal species face extinction, weakening ecosystems' ability to function and adapt. The three crises feed one another, raising environmental risks and causing global economic loss. The framework resembles other broad views of human impact, such as the limits mapped in {{ref:nature-eco-597}}.

nature-found-029.title: Managing the planet's land, water and air for the long run
nature-found-029.text: Feeding humanity takes about 38% of Earth's land surface and about 20% of its net primary productivity, the new plant growth its ecosystems produce. Since the Neolithic Revolution, human consumption has cut the world's forest cover by about 47%. Sustainability and environmental management means running the oceans, fresh water, land and atmosphere at global scale by sustainability principles. How land is split between cities, farms, forest and pasture strongly affects the global cycles of water, carbon and nitrogen. Biodiversity loss stems largely from habitat loss, as natural capital is converted into man-made capital.

nature-found-021.title: Accommodative capacity: a sharper measure of what water can take
nature-found-021.text: Assimilative capacity proved too slippery for some regulators. Inconsistency in how it was used led NOAA and the EPA, two US government agencies, to restrict the term. Accommodative capacity was proposed as a less ambiguous alternative, because its uses are defined more in numbers. It is the rate at which waste can be added to a body of water while keeping contaminants below levels that cause unacceptable biological harm.

openers.found: Every economy rests on a stock it did not build: rocks, soils, air, water and all living things. That stock is called natural capital, and the many benefits people draw from it are called ecosystem services. This part begins with the basics: what an ecosystem is, how varied life is, and how nature's benefits are sorted. It then asks why that foundation is wearing down, in an age when humanity has become a force that changes the whole planet.
openers.nature-as-the-economy-s-foundation: Life on Earth fills a thin zone, the biosphere, built from countless ecosystems. Each one links living things to their non-living surroundings through flows of energy and nutrients. People draw benefits from them all the time, from food and clean water to beauty and spiritual meaning. This chapter names those benefits, counts the stock that yields them, and asks what it would take to keep both going long into the future.

reviews.nature-as-the-economy-s-foundation: Ecosystems, joined together in the biosphere, make up the stock called natural capital. That stock yields ecosystem services, sorted into provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting groups, and a rich variety of life often helps keep them steady. Yet people have altered about 70% of Earth's land, fresh water is running short, and pollution, climate change and biodiversity loss feed one another. Efforts to count nature, from the Natural Capital Protocol to national environmental accounts, run into a hard question: whether nature should carry a money value at all. Short-term thinking makes the long-term goal of sustainability harder still.
